chapter: The Paradise and life in Queens
title: Church, the Muslim movement and refusing heroin
summary: He never went to church; he explains why he did not follow friends like Art Blakey and Idrees Sulieman into Islam or into heroin.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Had you gone to church at all, was church a part of the picture at all?

No. No, it wasn't. No, I never went to church. I'm not gonna say I did when I didn't. But I was aware of the church and some towns, you know, if you meet a lady fair, if you're with her for a few days and, "Let's go to church," then you go to church, you know. One of them things. (laughter)
In the '40's there were a number of musicians, I'm sure you knew some of them, who became Muslims. There was a movement that started at that time...

Yes, Art Blake[ey] and Idrees Sulieman and a lot of guys. There was a movement. But I listened to 'em and I says, "Well, I don't feel that I should do that." Just like when the guys start shootin' heroin in their arms, you know, I wasn't, you know, they're still my friends but I said I wasn't goin' to do that. You know what I mean. And that Muslim thing, you know, everyone was excited about it and changin' their names and you'll become a real citizen of America, but it didn't work out like that, you know what I mean. When they did that they just ended up stickin' out like sore thumbs and so they had to live with that. That's quite a thing, you know, because you change your religion and a new faith and now people are more tolerant of things like that. You got Jabbar and a couple of football players and several basketball players and, I mean, what the heck, people don't pay it no mind no more, but at that time, "What the heck you doin', this American way is all right, what are you doin' this for?"
